entries.f956b59ab4ca281558adb6db6307c9f081036341: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10628"/><div sID="gen18996" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10628"/>46. Copied from <reference osisRef="Num.21.29">Nu 21:29</reference>. <div eID="gen18996" type="x-p"/>
entries.756c6039c101ad5eb3b8e30c1f8ea0aacecb674e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10629"/><div sID="gen18997" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10629"/>47. Restoration promised to Moab, for the sake of righteous Lot, their progenitor (<reference osisRef="Gen.19.37">Ge 19:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.20.6">Ex 20:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.89.30-Ps.89.33">Psa 89:30-33</reference>). Compare as to Egypt, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.26">Jr 46:26</reference>; Ammon, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.6">Jr 49:6</reference>; Elam, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.39">Jr 49:39</reference>. Gospel blessings, temporal and spiritual, to the Gentiles in the last days, are intended. <chapter eID="Jer.48"/>

entries.5f688123baaac1949acbb90a1d691a43fb93f0ce: <div eID="gen30578" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen30579" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30580" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30580" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30579" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30581" type="x-p"/> The following prophecy concerning the Moabites is supposed to have had its accomplishment during the long siege of Tyre in the reign of Nebuchadnezzar. The whole of this chapter is poetry of the first order. The distress of the cities of Moab, with which it opens, is finely described. The cries of one ruined city resound to those of another, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.1-Jer.48.3">Jer 48:1-3</reference>. The doleful helpless cry of the children is heard, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.4">Jer 48:4</reference>; the highways, on either hand, resound with the voice of weeping, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.5">Jer 48:5</reference>; and the few that remain resemble a blasted tree in the wide howling waste, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.6">Jer 48:6</reference>. Chemosh, the chief god of the Moabites, and the capital figure in the triumph, is represented as carried off in chains, with all his trumpery of priests and officers, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.7">Jer 48:7</reference>. The desolation of the country shall be so general and sudden that, by a strong figure, it is intimated that there shall be no possibility of escape, except it be in the speediest flight, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.8">Jer 48:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.9">Jer 48:9</reference>. And some idea may be formed of the dreadful wickedness of this people from the consideration that the prophet, under the immediate inspiration of the Almighty, pronounces a curse on those who do the work of the Lord negligently, in not proceeding to their utter extermination, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.10">Jer 48:10</reference>. The subject is then diversified by an elegant and well-supported comparison, importing that the Moabites increased in insolence and pride in proportion to the duration of their prosperity, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.11">Jer 48:11</reference>; but this prosperity is declared to be nearly at an end; the destroyer is already commissioned against Moab, and his neighbors called to sing the usual lamentation at his funeral, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.13-Jer.48.18">Jer 48:13-18</reference>. The prophet then represents some of the women of Aroer and Ammon, (the extreme borders of Moab), standing in the highways, and asking the fugitives of Moab, What intelligence? They inform him of the complete discomfiture of Moab, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.19-Jer.48.24">Jer 48:19-24</reference>, and of the total annihilation of its political existence, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.25">Jer 48:25</reference>. The Divine judgments about to fall upon Moab are farther represented under the expressive metaphor of a cup of intoxicating liquor, by which he should become an object of derision because of his intolerable pride, his magnifying himself against Jehovah, and his great contempt for the children of Israel in the day of their calamity, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.26">Jer 48:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.27">Jer 48:27</reference>. The prophet then points out the great distress of Moab by a variety of striking figures, viz., by the failure of the customary rejoicings at the end of harvest, by the mournful sort of music used at funerals, by the signs which were expressive among the ancients of deep mourning, as shaving the head, clipping the beard, cutting the flesh, and wearing sackcloth; and by the methods of catching wild beasts in toils, and by the terror and pitfall, vv. 28-46. In the close of the chapter it is intimated that a remnant shall be preserved from this general calamity whose descendants shall be prosperous in the latter days, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.47">Jer 48:47</reference>. <div eID="gen30581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30582" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen30582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30583" type="x-p"/> Against Moab - This was delivered some time after the destruction of Jerusalem. The Moabites were in the neighborhood of the Ammonites, and whatever evils fell on the one would naturally involve the other. See <reference osisRef="Isa.15.1-Isa.15.9">Isa 15:1-9</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.16.1-Isa.16.14">Isa 16:1-14</reference> on this same subject. <div eID="gen30583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30584" type="x-p"/> Wo unto Nebo! for it is spoiled - This was a city in the tribe of Reuben, afterwards possessed by the Moabites. It probably had its name from Nebo, one of the principal idols of the Moabites. <div eID="gen30584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30585" type="x-p"/> Kiriathaim - Another city of the Moabites. <div eID="gen30585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30586" type="x-p"/> Misgab is confounded - There is no place of this name known, and therefore several learned men translate המשגב hammisgab, literally, The high tower, or fortress, which may apply to Kiriathaim, or any other high and well-fortified place.
entries.aacb6e79c98cba40f0e50fa9a6618c5d77575932: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen30586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30587" type="x-p"/> No more praise of Moab - "The glory of Moab, that it had never been conquered," (Dahler), is now at an end. Dr. Blayney translates: - "Moab shall have no more glorying in Heshbon; They have devised evil against her (saying.)" <div eID="gen30587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30588" type="x-p"/> And this most certainly is the best translation of the original. He has marked also a double paronomasia in this and the next verse, a figure in which the prophets delight; בחשבון חשבו becheshbon chashebu "in Cheshbon they have devised," and מדמן תדמי madmen tiddommi, "Madmena, thou shalt be dumb."
entries.f6f20f5daa41d34a1da5fa6f33878697b63243bd: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen30588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30589" type="x-p"/> Horonaim - Another city of Moab, near to Luhith. At this latter place the hill country of Moab commenced. "It is a place," says Dahler, "situated upon a height between Areopolis and Zoar."
entries.29a0cb29761d039a1d4fa467a1de888484894a5c: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen30589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30590" type="x-p"/> Flee, save your lives - The enemy is in full pursuit of you. <div eID="gen30590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30591" type="x-p"/> Be like the heath - כערוער caaroer, "like Aroer;" which some take for a city, others for a blasted or withered tree. It is supposed that a place of this name lay towards the north, in the land of the Ammonites, on a branch of the river Jabbok; surrounded by deserts. Save yourselves by getting into the wilderness, where the pursuing foe will scarcely think it worth his while to follow you, as the wilderness itself must soon destroy you.
entries.2784518e32616b8fcc42ea37f0b97d05cdf29884: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen30591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30592" type="x-p"/> Chemosh shall go forth into captivity - The grand national idol of the Moabites, <reference osisRef="Num.21.29">Num 21:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jdg.11.24">Jdg 11:24</reference>. Ancient idolaters used to take their gods with them to the field of battle. This was probably in imitation of the Israelites, who took the ark with them in such cases.
entries.8090327a0ff8d07737b0c9859727304d829fc823: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen30592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30593" type="x-p"/> Give wings unto Moab - There is no hope in resistance, and to escape requires the speediest flight. I cannot conceive how Dahler came to translate thus: Tirez Moab par les chevaux, "Drag Moab away by the hair of the head."
entries.28a9a453b709b59fd000dbff66aafc1378385ec9: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen30593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30594" type="x-p"/> Cursed be he that doeth the work of the Lord deceitfully - Moab is doomed to destruction, and the Lord pronounces a curse on their enemies if they do not proceed to utter extirpation. God is the Author of life, and has a sovereign right to dispose of it as he pleases; and these had forfeited theirs long ago by their idolatry and other crimes.
entries.2f1d7db29b9def1045519bb4cd88407934968bb8: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen30594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30595" type="x-p"/> Moab hath been at ease - The metaphor here is taken from the mode of preserving wines. They let them rest upon their lees for a considerable time, as this improves them both in strength and flavour; and when this is sufficiently done, they rack, or pour them off into other vessels. Moab had been very little molested by war since he was a nation; he had never gone out of his own land. Though some had been carried away by Shalmaneser forty years before this, he has had neither wars nor captivity. <div eID="gen30595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30596" type="x-p"/> Therefore his taste remained in him - Still carrying on the allusion to the curing of wines; by resting long upon the lees, the taste and smell are both improved. See the note on <reference osisRef="Isa.25.6">Isa 25:6</reference>.
entries.cb3e398cef6c26375f175b0979e796fb753b5fca: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen30596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30597" type="x-p"/> I will send unto him wanderers that shall cause him to wander - Dr. Blayney renders צעים tsaim, tilters; those who elevate one end of the wine cask when nearly run out that the remains of the liquor may be the more effectually drawn off at the cock. And this seems to be well supported by the following words, - <div eID="gen30597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30598" type="x-p"/> And shall empty his vessels - I will send such as will carry the whole nation into captivity.
entries.ed4be5c5097e21b837c97800da9bcc7d4071c983: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen30598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30599" type="x-p"/> Beth-el their confidence - Alluding to the golden calves which Jeroboam had there set up, and commanded all the Israelites to worship.
entries.0c93d0ad80152b8d8b01b40fc5c4d3bac5c81298: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen30599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30600" type="x-p"/> How is the strong staff broken - The scepter. The sovereignty of Moab is destroyed.
entries.800dc112a921cd8a224995b95fd50713945dce10: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen30600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30601" type="x-p"/> That dost inhabit Dibon - This was anciently a city of the Reubenites, afterwards inhabited by the Moabites, about two leagues north of the river Arnon, and about six to the east of the Dead Sea. - Dahler.
entries.526906456fc358a835db8503d9959e494c1110bd: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen30601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30602" type="x-p"/> O inhabitant of Aroer - See the note on <reference osisRef="Jer.48.6">Jer 48:6</reference> (note). This place, being at a greater distance, is counselled to watch for its own safety, and inquire of every passenger, What is done? that it may know when to pack up and be gone.
entries.510dd823ec08d1cd6d046dd6ac58b20bf87ea834: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen30602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30603" type="x-p"/> Tell ye it in Arnon - Apprize the inhabitants there that the territories of Moab are invaded, and the country about to be destroyed, that they may provide for their own safety.
entries.a5e1da37ec8aa739cd607960431c080377240214: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen30603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30604" type="x-p"/> Upon Holon, etc. - All these were cities of the Moabites, but several of them are mentioned in no other place.
entries.93cf1946fa465ced2d502463d356b4677d35ab50: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen30604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30605" type="x-p"/> The horn of Moab is cut off, and his arm is broken - His political and physical powers are no more.
entries.64db8cc27171b321a012cdcd45e919d131f8e962: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen30605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30606" type="x-p"/> Was not Israel a derision unto thee? - Didst thou not mock my people, and say their God was no better than the gods of other nations? See <reference osisRef="Eze.25.8">Eze 25:8</reference>. <div eID="gen30606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30607" type="x-p"/> Was he found among thieves? - Did the Israelites come to rob and plunder you? Why then mock them, and rejoice at their desolation, when their enemies prevailed over them? This the Lord particularly resents.
entries.7e56c925f3abcac5851de1724a028f5a4929897d: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen30607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30608" type="x-p"/> Dwell in the rock - Go to the most inaccessible places in the mountains. <div eID="gen30608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30609" type="x-p"/> The hole's mouth - And into the most secret eaves and holes of the earth.
entries.4f4eb0b0b4d9f3986cbc8ca4d4efe9ef64eaf186: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen30609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30610" type="x-p"/> The pride of Moab - See on <reference osisRef="Isa.16.1">Isa 16:1</reference> (note).
entries.1aec90a325e060142073b5aa9f91242f14daa0c5: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen30610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30611" type="x-p"/> O vine of Sibmah - See on <reference osisRef="Isa.16.8">Isa 16:8</reference> (note).
entries.60c933b5e1c25846e3b2ca318f22e1657e9c8a92: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen30611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30612" type="x-p"/> As a heifer of three years old - Which runs lowing from place to place in search of her calf, which is lost or taken from her.
entries.70f14c4c3bc3f465de7473dc8ae96ea5157e2db1: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen30612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30613" type="x-p"/> For every head shall be bald - These, as we have seen before, were signs of the deepest distress and desolation.
entries.ae6dcf734810ed1eef8c3198fd9d41ea2301a225: <hi type="bold">Verse 40</hi> <div eID="gen30613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30614" type="x-p"/> He shall fly as an eagle - The enemy will pounce upon him, carry him off, and tear him to pieces.
entries.c17102d1d5a484baf9c14f4c8a74e05cae8283d5: <hi type="bold">Verse 42</hi> <div eID="gen30614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30615" type="x-p"/> Moab shall be destroyed from being a people - They shall not have a king or civil governor: and I doubt whether there be any evidence that they were ever reinstated in their national character. They were captivated by the Chaldeans; and probably many returned with the Jews on the edict of Cyrus: but as to their being an independent nation after this, where is the positive proof?
entries.7b3cf3f9007cbc30739d31106d226524c94f298f: <hi type="bold">Verse 43</hi> <div eID="gen30615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30616" type="x-p"/> Fear, and the pit, and the snare - See the note on <reference osisRef="Isa.24.17">Isa 24:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.18">Isa 24:18</reference>.
entries.87f9f852eb01b540ec6f69ae57d99ffe5e851d4b: <hi type="bold">Verse 45</hi> <div eID="gen30616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30617" type="x-p"/> They that fled stood under the shadow of Heshbon - Heshbon being a fortified place, they who were worsted in the fight fled to it, and rallied under its walls; but, instead of safety, they found themselves disappointed, betrayed, and ruined. See <reference osisRef="Jer.48.2">Jer 48:2</reference> (note), and the note there. <div eID="gen30617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30618" type="x-p"/> But a fire shall come forth out of Heshbon - Jeremiah has borrowed this part of his discourse from an ancient poet quoted by Moses, <reference osisRef="Num.21.28">Num 21:28</reference> (note); where see the notes. <div eID="gen30618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30619" type="x-p"/> The crown of the head - The choicest persons of the whole nation.
entries.b3973e881f665b220fae4c8548db823d3778093d: <hi type="bold">Verse 46</hi> <div eID="gen30619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30620" type="x-p"/> The people of Chemosh - The Moabites, who worshipped Chemosh as their supreme god.
entries.439dc26043e8122fdfb904d0b90f3db326df29f3: <hi type="bold">Verse 47</hi> <div eID="gen30620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30621" type="x-p"/> Will I bring again the captivity of Moab in the latter days - I have already expressed doubts (see <reference osisRef="Jer.48.42">Jer 48:42</reference>) whether the Moabites were ever restored to their national distinction. The expressions in this chapter, relative to their total destruction as a people, are so strong and so frequent, that they leave little room for a limited interpretation. That many of them returned on the edict of Cyrus by virtue of which the Jews were restored, I doubt not; but neither the Ammonites, Moabites, Philistines, nor even the Jews themselves were ever restored to their national consequence. Perhaps the restoration spoken of here which was to take place in the latter days, may mean the conversion of these people, in their existing remnants, to the faith of the Gospel. Several judicious interpreters are of this opinion. The Moabites were partially restored; but never, as far as I have been able to learn, to their national consequence. Their conversion to the Christian faith must be the main end designed by this prophecy.  <chapter eID="Jer.48"/> <div eID="gen30621" type="x-p"/>

entries.c556f96d9dc450f58f6acb7356d3e5e962bac3de: <reference osisRef="Jer.48.1-Jer.48.8">Jer 48:1-8</reference> <hi type="italic">Calamities to come on Moab. -</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.48.1">Jer 48:1</reference> <hi type="italic">. "Thus saith Jahveh of hosts, the God of Israel, Woe to Nebo, for it is laid waste! Kiriathaim is come to dishonour, it is taken: the fortress is come to dishonour and broken down.</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.48.2">Jer 48:2</reference> <hi type="italic">. Moab’s glory is no more. In Heshbon they have devised evil against her, [saying], Come, and let us cut her off from [being] a nation: thou also, O Madmen, art brought to silence; the sword shall go after thee.</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.48.3">Jer 48:3</reference> <hi type="italic">. A sound of crying from Horonaim, desolation and great destruction.</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.48.4">Jer 48:4</reference> <hi type="italic">. Moab is destroyed; her little ones have caused a cry to be heard.</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.48.5">Jer 48:5</reference> <hi type="italic">. For they ascend the ascent of Luhith with weeping - weeping: for on the descent of Horonaim the enemies have heard a cry of destruction.</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.48.6">Jer 48:6</reference> <hi type="italic">. Flee, save your life! and be like one destitute in the wilderness.</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.48.7">Jer 48:7</reference> <hi type="italic">. For, because they trust [was] in thy works, and in thy treasures, thou also shalt be taken; and Chemosh shall go into captivity, his priests and his princes together.</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.48.8">Jer 48:8</reference> <hi type="italic">. The destroyer shall come to every city, and no city shall escape; and the valley shall perish, and the plain shall be laid waste, as Jahveh hath said."</hi> <div eID="gen14383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14384" type="x-p"/> With the exclamation "Woe!" Jeremiah transports the hearers of the word of God at once into the midst of the catastrophe which is to come on Moab; this is with the view of humbling the pride of this people, and chastening them for their sins. The woe is uttered over Nebo, but holds also of the towns named afterwards. Nebo is not the mountain of that name (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.49">Deu 32:49</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.34.1">Deu 34:1</reference>), but the city, which probably did not lie far from the peak in the mountain-range of Abarim, which bore the same name (Num 32:3, Num 32:38; <reference osisRef="Isa.15.2">Isa 15:2</reference>), although in the <hi type="italic">Onomasticon, s.v.</hi> Ναβαῦ, the situation of the mountain is given as being six Roman miles from Heshbon, towards the west, and <hi type="italic">s.v.</hi> Ναβώρ, that of the city, eight Roman miles south from Heshbon, for both accounts point to a situation in the south-west. The Arab. name <hi type="italic">nba=</hi> is still applied to some ruins; cf. Robinson’s <hi type="italic">Palestine</hi>, iii. p. 170. "Kiriathaim is taken." The site of this town, mentioned as early as <reference osisRef="Gen.14.5">Gen 14:5</reference>, has been fixed, since the time of Burckhardt, as that of a mass of ruins called et Teim, about five miles south of Heshbon; but Dietrich, in <hi type="italic">Merx' Archiv</hi>. i. S. 337ff., has shown this is incorrect. According to Eusebius, in his <hi type="italic">Onomasticon</hi>, Kiriathaim lay ten Roman miles to the west of Medeba: this suits not merely the position of <hi type="italic">et Teim</hi>, but also the ruins of Kereyat south-west from Medeba, on the ridge of Mount Attarus, a little to the south of M'kaur (<hi type="italic">Machaerus</hi>), and of Baara in the <hi type="italic">Wady Zerka Maein</hi>, where also is the plain mentioned in <reference osisRef="Gen.14.5">Gen 14:5</reference>, either in the plain stretching direct east from <hi type="italic">Kereyat</hi> between Wady Zerka Maein and Wady Wal, or south-east in the beautiful plain <hi type="italic">el Kura</hi>, described by Burckhardt, p. 371ff., between the Wal and the Mojeb. Nebo and Kiriathaim lay on the eastern border of the high range of mountains, and seem to be comprehended under המּשׂגּב, "the height, the high fortress," in the third clause of <reference osisRef="Jer.48.1">Jer 48:1</reference>, as the representatives of the mountain country of Moab. Various expositors, certainly, take the word as a proper name designating an elevated region; Graf and Nägelsbach take it to be a name of Kir-Moab (Kir-heres, Kir-haresheth, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.31">Jer 48:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.36">Jer 48:36</reference>), the chief fortress in the country, the modern <hi type="italic">Kerek</hi> in the southern part of Moab; but no valid proof has been adduced. By "the height" Hitzig understands the highlands, which learn of the fall of these towns in the lowlands, and feel this disgrace that has come on Moab, but have not yet themselves been taken. But this view is untenable, because the towns of Nebo and Kiriathaim are not situated in the level country. Again, since הובשׁה is common to the two clauses, the distinction between נלכּדה and חתּה could hardly be pressed so far as to make the latter the opposite of the former, in the sense of being still unconquered. The meaning rather is, that through Nebo’s being laid waste, and the capture of Kiriathaim, the fortress on which the Moabites trusted is no more. And to this <reference osisRef="Jer.48.3">Jer 48:3</reference> appropriately adds, "the boasting of Moab is gone," i.e., Moab has no more ground for boasting. "In Heshbon they (the enemy, or the conquerors) plot evil against Moab." Heshbon was formerly the capital of the Amorite kingdom of Sihon (Num 21:26; <reference osisRef="Deut.2.24">Deu 2:24</reference>, etc.), and was assigned to the tribe of Reuben (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.17">Jos 13:17</reference>); but because it lay on the boundary of the territory belonging to the tribe, it was given up to the Gadites, and set apart as a Levitical city (<reference osisRef="Josh.21.37">Jos 21:37</reference>). It lay ten Roman miles east from the Jordan, opposite Jericho, almost intermediate between the Arnon and the Jabbok, and is still pointed out, though in ruins, under the old name <hi type="italic">Heshbân</hi> (see on Num 32:37). At the time of Jeremiah it was taken possession of by the Ammonites (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.3">Jer 49:3</reference>), consequently it was the frontier town of the Moabite territory at that time; and being such, it is here named as the town where the enemy, coming from the north, deliberate regarding the conquest of Moab - "meditate evil," i.e., decide upon conquest and devastation. The suffix of עליה refers to Moab as a country, and hence is feminine; cf. v. 4. "We will destroy it (Moab) מגּוי, so that it shall no longer be a nation." Just as in בּחשׁבּון חשׁבוּ there is a play on the words, so is there also in the expression מדמן תּדּמּי which follows. This very circumstance forms an argument for taking Madmen as a proper name, instead of an appellative, as Venema and Hitzig have done, after the example of the lxx: "Yea, thou shalt be destroyed (and made into) a dunghill." In support of this rendering they point to 2Ki 10:27; Ezr 6:11. But the verb דּמם, in its meaning, ill accords with מדמן in the sense of a dung-heap, and in this case there would be no foundation for a play upon the words (Graf). It is no proof of the non-existence of a place called Madmen in Moab, that it is not mentioned elsewhere; Madmena in the tribe of Benjamin (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.31">Isa 10:31</reference>), and Madmanna in Judah (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.31">Jos 15:31</reference>), are also mentioned but once. These passages rather show that the name <hi type="italic">Madmen</hi> was not uncommon; and it was perhaps with reference to this name that Isaiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.25.10">Isa 25:10</reference>) chose the figure of the dunghill. דּמם, to be silent, means, in the Niphal, to be brought to silence, be exterminated, perish; cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.49.26">Jer 49:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.37">Jer 25:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.8.14">Jer 8:14</reference>, etc. As to the form תּדּמּי instead of תּדּמּי , cf. Ewald, §140, <hi type="italic">b</hi>; Gesenius, §67, Rem. 5. The following clause refers to Madmen: "after thee shall the sword go;" cf. Jer 9:15.
entries.254dffca34a5913effa7fcb7fdfb9480a30fc4e5: <reference osisRef="Jer.48.9">Jer 48:9</reference> <hi type="italic">Moab is laid waste, and its inhabitants carried captive. -</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.48.9">Jer 48:9</reference> <hi type="italic">. "Give pinions to Moab, for he will flee and get away, and his cities shall become a waste, with no one dwelling in them.</hi> Jer 48:10. <hi type="italic">Cursed is he that doeth the work of Jahveh negligently, and cursed is he that restraineth his sword from blood.</hi> Jer 48:11. <hi type="italic">Moab hath been at ease from his youth, and lay still upon his lees; he was not poured out from vessel to vessel, neither hath he gone into captivity, therefore his taste hath remained in him, and his smell hath not changed.</hi> Jer 48:12. <hi type="italic">Therefore, behold, days come, saith Jahveh, when I will send to him those who pour out, and they shall pour him out; and they shall empty his vessels, and break their bottles.</hi> Jer 48:13. <hi type="italic">And Moab shall be ashamed of Chemosh, as the house of Israel was ashamed of Bethel their confidence.</hi> Jer 48:14. <hi type="italic">How can ye say, We are mighty, and men of valour for the war?</hi> Jer 48:15. <hi type="italic">Moab is laid waste, and people ascend into his cities, and the choice of his young men go down to the slaughter, saith the King, whose name is Jahveh of hosts."</hi> <div eID="gen14388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14389" type="x-p"/> The devastation will come so suddenly, that Moab, in order to escape it, uses wings for enabling him to flee from it. The request "give" is not ironical, but a mere rhetorical employment of the idea that wings would be necessary in order to escape. ציץ, which elsewhere means a flower, here signifies wings or waving plumes, as in the Targum on <reference osisRef="Ps.139.9">Psa 139:9</reference>, and in the Rabbinical writings. נצא, written with א for the sake of obtaining similarity of sound, stands for נצה = נצץ, to flee.
entries.17c6f8b25c77fb7ffe9610ef59f09595e87f529d: <reference osisRef="Jer.48.10-Jer.48.12">Jer 48:10-12</reference> <div eID="gen14389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14390" type="x-p"/> The devastation is a work of the Lord, and those who execute it must carry out the divine decree, so that they may not bring the curse upon themselves. The first clause is taken quite generally: the more exact specification of the work of the Lord follows in the second clause; it is the employment of the sword against Moab. "His sword" does not mean Jahveh’s, but the sword carried by the devastator. רמיּה is used adverbially, but not in the sense of "deceitfully," rather "carelessly, negligently;" cf. כּף רמיּה, <reference osisRef="Prov.10.4">Pro 10:4</reference>; Pro 12:24. In <reference osisRef="Jer.48.11">Jer 48:11</reference> follows the reason why the judgment has necessarily come on Moab. Moab is compared to old wine that has lain long on its lees, and thereby preserved its flavour and smell unchanged. The taste and odour of Moab signify his disposition towards other nations, particularly towards Israel, the people of God. Good wine becomes stronger and more juicy by lying pretty long on its lees (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.25.6">Isa 25:6</reference>); inferior wine, however, becomes thereby more harsh and thick. The figure is used here in the latter sense, after Zep 1:12. Moab’s disposition towards Israel was harsh and bitter; the people were arrogant and proud (Jer 48:29.; <reference osisRef="Isa.16.6">Isa 16:6</reference>), and so hostile towards Israel, that they sought every opportunity of injuring them (see above, p. 385f., and the comments on <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.2">2Sa 8:2</reference>). From his youth, i.e., from the time when Moab, after subduing the Emims (<reference osisRef="Deut.2.10">Deu 2:10</reference>), had established himself in his own land, or had become enrolled among the nations of history, - from that time forward had he remained undisturbed in his own land, i.e., without being driven out of it, had not gone into captivity (as is shown by the figure of the wine poured from one vessel into another). In this way there is a qualification made of the general statement that he remains at rest on his lees, and undisturbed. For Moab has often carried on wars, and even suffered many defeats, but has never yet been driven from his own land; nor had the temporary dependence on Israel exercised any transforming influence on the ordinary life of the people, for they were simply made tributary. This quiet continuance in the country is to cease. The God of Israel "will send to them cellarmen (Germ. <hi type="italic">Schröter</hi>), who shall bring them out of the cellar" (Germ. <hi type="italic">ausschroten</hi>), as Luther translates Jer 48:12. "<hi type="italic">Schröter</hi>" are men who bring the wine-casks out of the cellar; for "<hi type="italic">schroten</hi>" means to bring out heavy burdens, especially full casks on a strong kind of hand-barrow (Germ. <hi type="italic">Hebewerkzeug</hi>), like a ladder in appearance. צעים (from צעה, to bend, incline) are those who incline a barrel or vessel for the purpose or pouring out its contents. These will not merely empty the vessels, but also break the pitchers; i.e., not merely carry away the Moabites, but also break down their political organization, and destroy their social arrangements.
entries.4c60d08b34b2e37ac412749edb77221640a6f204: <reference osisRef="Jer.48.13-Jer.48.15">Jer 48:13-15</reference> <div eID="gen14390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14391" type="x-p"/> In this way Moab will come to dishonour through his god Chemosh, i.e., experience his powerlessness and nothingness, and perish with him, just as Israel (the ten tribes) came to dishonour through Bethel, i.e., through their golden calf at Bethel. As to the form מבטחם, with Segol in the pretone, cf. Ewald, §70, <hi type="italic">a</hi>; Olshausen, <hi type="italic">Gram</hi>. S. 377. Moab will then be no longer able to boast of his valour; this is the meaning of the question in <reference osisRef="Jer.48.14">Jer 48:14</reference> : on this term in the address, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.2.23">Jer 2:23</reference>; Jer 8:8. In <reference osisRef="Jer.48.15">Jer 48:15</reference> it is further stated that the result will show this: "Moab is laid waste." ועריה עלה is variously interpreted. An explanation which has met with much acceptance, but which nevertheless is really untenable, is founded on Jdg 20:40 ("The whole city went up towards heaven" i.e., in smoke and fire): "As for his cities, fire or smoke ascends;" but there is no mention here either of smoke or fire. Kimchi long ago came near the truth when he sought to find the subject שׁדד in shudad שׁדּד: "and the devastator comes against his cities." However, the contrast between עלה and ירדוּ is not fully brought out in this way: it is better to leave the subject indeterminate: "and his cities they climb" (Kueper), or: "they go up to his cities" (Böttcher, <hi type="italic">Neue Aehrenlese</hi>, ii. 163). The enemy who mounts the cities is evidently intended. The change שׁדּד into שׁדד is both unnecessary and unsuitable; but J. D. Michaelis, Ewald, Dahler, Graf, after making the alteration, translate, "The destroyer of Moab and of his cities draws near." Hitzig justly remarks, in opposition to this conjecture: "There is nothing to justify the mere placing of the subject at the head of the sentence (contrast <reference osisRef="Jer.48.8">Jer 48:8</reference>, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Jer.48.18">Jer 48:18</reference></hi>); besides, one does not see why the cities of Moab are distinguished from Moab itself; and cf. 20 <hi type="italic">b</hi>." ירד לבּטח, "to sink down to the slaughter," cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.50.27">Jer 50:27</reference>; and on this use of ירד, Isa 34:7. The enemy <hi type="italic">ascends</hi> into the cities, the young soldiers of Moab <hi type="italic">descend</hi> to the shambles. This threatening is enforced by the addition, "saith the King," etc. Jahveh is called the King, in contrast with the belief of the Moabites, that their god Chemosh was the king of his people (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.48.7">Jer 48:7</reference>). The true King of the Moabites also is Jahveh, the God of hosts, i.e., the Ruler of the whole world.
entries.5b7cebf05e34fdb5071ae6b819847480dbfef76a: <reference osisRef="Jer.48.16-Jer.48.17">Jer 48:16-17</reference> <hi type="italic">Moab’s glory is departed. -</hi> Jer 48:16. <hi type="italic">"The destruction of Moab is near to come, and his trouble hastens rapidly.</hi> Jer 48:17. <hi type="italic">Bewail him, all [ye who are] round about him, and all who know his name! Say, How the rod of strength is broken, the staff of majesty!</hi> Jer 48:18. <hi type="italic">Come down from [thy] glory, and sit in the drought, [thou] inhabitants, daughter of Dibon; for the destroyer of Moab hath come up against thee, he hath destroyed thy strongholds.</hi> Jer 48:19. <hi type="italic">Stand by the way, and watch, O inhabitants of Aroer! ask him who flees, and her that has escaped; say, What has happened?</hi> Jer 48:20. <hi type="italic">Moab is ashamed, for it is broken down: howl and cry out; tell it in Arnon, that Moab is laid waste.</hi> Jer 48:21. <hi type="italic">And judgment hath come upon the country of the plain, upon Holon, and upon Jahzah, and upon Mephaath,</hi> Jer 48:22. <hi type="italic">And upon Dibon, and upon Nebo, and upon Beth-diblathaim,</hi> Jer 48:23. <hi type="italic">And upon Kirjathaim, and upon Beth-gamul, and upon Beth-meon,</hi> Jer 48:24. <hi type="italic">And upon Kerioth, and upon Bozrah, and upon all the cities of the land of Moab, those that are far off and those that are near.</hi> Jer 48:25. <hi type="italic">The horn of Moab is cut off, ad his arm is broken, saith Jahveh."</hi> <div eID="gen14391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14392" type="x-p"/> The downfall of Moab will soon begin. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Jer.48.16">Jer 48:16</reference></hi> is an imitation of <reference osisRef="Deut.32.35">Deu 32:35</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.13.22">Isa 13:22</reference>; Isa 56:1. The fall of the Moabite power and glory will be so terrible, that all the nations, near ad distant, will have pity on him. The summons to lament, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.17">Jer 48:17</reference>, is not a mockery, but is seriously meant, for the purpose of expressing the idea that the downfall of so mighty and glorious a power will rouse compassion. The environs of Moab are the neighbouring nations, and "those who know his name" are those who live far off, and have only heard about him. The staff, the sceptre, is the emblem of authority; cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.19.11-Ezek.19.12">Eze 19:11-12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.19.14">Eze 19:14</reference>, and Psa 110:2.
entries.13d78f7f6b9b4487b508d0e82146c3923013d019: <reference osisRef="Jer.48.18-Jer.48.20">Jer 48:18-20</reference> <div eID="gen14392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14393" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Jer.48.18-Jer.48.25">Jer 48:18-25</reference> is further described the downfall of this strong and glorious power. The inhabitants if Dibon are to come down from their glory and sit in misery; those of Aroer are to ask the fugitives what has happened, that they may learn that the whole table-land on to the Arnon has been taken by the enemy; and they are to howl over the calamity. The idea presented in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Jer.48.18">Jer 48:18</reference></hi> is an imitation of that in <reference osisRef="Isa.47.1">Isa 47:1</reference>, "Come down, O daughter of Babylon, sit in the dust;" but רדי is intensified by the addition of מכּבוד, and וּשׁבי על is changed into  וּשׁבי בצּמא (the <hi type="italic">Kethib</hi> ישׁבי has evidently been written by mistake for וּשׁבי, the <hi type="italic">Qeri</hi>). צמא elsewhere means "thirst;" but "sit down in the thirst" would be too strange an expression; hence צמא must here have the meaning of  צמא, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.3">Isa 44:3</reference>, "the thirsty arid land:" thus it remains a question whether we should point the word צמא, or take צמא as another form of צמא, as חלב sa ,צîא fo mro is of חלב, Eze 23:19. There is no sufficient reason why Hitzig and Ewald should give the word a meaning foreign to it, from the Arabic or Syriac. Dibon lay about four miles north from the Arnon, at the foot of a mountain, in a very beautiful plain, where, under the name of <hi type="italic">Dibân</hi>, many traces of walls, and a well by the wayside, hewn out of the rock, are still to be found (Seetzen, i. S. 409f.). Hence it must have been well provided with water, even though we should be obliged to understand by "the water of Dimon" (Dibon), which Isaiah mentions (<reference osisRef="Isa.15.9">Isa 15:9</reference>), the river Arnon, which is about three miles off. The command to "sit down in an arid land" thus forms a suitable figure, representing the humiliation and devastation of Dibon. That the city was fortified, is evident from the mention of the fortifications in the last clause. ישׁבת , as in Jer 46:19. Aroer was situated on the north bank of the Arnon (<hi type="italic">Mojeb</hi>), where its ruins still remain, under the old name <hi type="italic">Arâ'ir</hi> (Burckhardt, p. 372). It was a frontier town, between the kingdom of Sihon (afterwards the territory of the Israelites) and the possession of the Moabites (<reference osisRef="Deut.2.36">Deu 2:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.3.12">Deu 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.4.48">Deu 4:48</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.12.2">Jos 12:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.13.9">Jos 13:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.13.16">Jos 13:16</reference>). But after the Moabites had regained the northern portion of their original territory, it lay in the midst of the land. The fugitives here represented as passing by are endeavouring, by crossing the Arnon, to escape from the enemy advancing from the north, and subduing the country before them. נס ונמלטה means fugitives of every kind. The co-ordination of the same word or synonymous terms in the masc. and fem. serves to generalize the idea; see on <reference osisRef="Isa.3.1">Isa 3:1</reference>, and Ewald, §172, <hi type="italic">c</hi>. In נמלטה  the tone is retracted through the influence of the distinctive accent; the form is participial. The question, "What has happened?" is answered in Jer 48:20. כּי חתּה, "for (= certainly) it is broken down." The <hi type="italic">Kethib</hi> הלילי וּזעקי must not be changed. Moab is addressed: with הגּידוּ is introduced the summons, addressed to individuals, to proclaim at the Arnon the calamity that has befallen the country to the north of that river.
entries.e9dde61811238ed02ce744c96b64a7151b1296cd: <reference osisRef="Jer.48.21-Jer.48.25">Jer 48:21-25</reference> <div eID="gen14393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14394" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Jer.48.21-Jer.48.24">Jer 48:21-24</reference> the general idea of Moab’s being laid waste is specialized by the enumeration of a long list of towns on which judgment has come. They are towns of ארץ המּישׁור, the table-land to the north of the Arnon, the names of which early all occur in the Pentateuch and Joshua as towns in the tribe of Reuben. But Holon is mentioned only here. According to Eusebius, in the <hi type="italic">Onomasticon, s.v.</hi>  ̓Ιεσσά, Jahzah was situated between Μηδαβῶν (<hi type="italic">Medeba</hi>) and Δηβοῦς (<hi type="italic">Dibon</hi>); according to Jerome, between <hi type="italic">Medeba</hi> and <hi type="italic">Debus</hi>, or <hi type="italic">Deblathai</hi>; but from Num 21:23, we conclude that it lay in an easterly direction, on the border of the desert, near the commencement of the Wady <hi type="italic">Wale</hi>. Mophaath or Mephaath, where, according to the <hi type="italic">Onomasticon</hi>, a Roman garrison was placed, on account of the near proximity of the desert, is to be sought for in the neighbourhood of Jahzah; see on Jos 13:18. As to Dibon, see on <reference osisRef="Jer.48.18">Jer 48:18</reference>; for Nebo, see on Jer 48:1. Beth-diblathaim is mentioned only in this passage. It is probably identical with Almon-diblathaim, Num 33:46, and to be sought for somewhere north from Dibon. For Kirjahthaim see Jer 48:1. Beth-gamul is nowhere else mentioned; its site, too, is unknown. Eli Smith, in Robinson’s <hi type="italic">Palestine</hi>, iii. App. p. 153, is inclined to recognise it in the ruins of <hi type="italic">Um-el-Jemel</hi>, lying on the southern boundary of the Hauran, about twenty miles south-west from Bozrah; but a consideration of the position shows that they cannot be the same. Beth-meon, or Baal-meon (Num 32:38), or more fully, Beth-baal-meon (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.17">Jos 13:17</reference>), lay about three miles south from Heshbon, where Burckhardt (p. 365) found some ruins called <hi type="italic">Mi-ûn</hi> (Robinson, iii. App. p. 170, <hi type="italic">Ma-în</hi>); see on Num 32:38. Kerioth, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.24">Jer 48:24</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.48.41">Jer 48:41</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Amos.2.2">Amo 2:2</reference>, is not to be identified with the ruins called <hi type="italic">Kereyath</hi> or <hi type="italic">Küreiyath</hi>, mentioned by Burckhardt (p. 367) and Seetzen (<hi type="italic">Reisen</hi>, ii. 342, iv. 384), as Ritter has assumed; for this Kereyath is more probably Kirjathaim (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.48.1">Jer 48:1</reference>). Rather, as is pretty fully proved by Dietrich (in <hi type="italic">Merx' Archiv.</hi> i. 320ff.), it is a synonym of <hi type="italic">Ar</hi>, the old capital of Moab, Num 22:36; and the plural form is to be accounted for by supposing that Ar was made up of two or several large portions. We find two great arguments supporting this position: (1.) When Ar, the capital, occurs among the names of the towns of Moab, as in the list of those in Reuben, <reference osisRef="Josh.13.16-Josh.13.21">Jos 13:16-21</reference>, and in the prophecy against Moab in Isaiah, Jer 15 and 16, where so many Moabitic towns are named, we find no mention of Kerioth; and on the other hand, where Kerioth is named as an important town in Moab, <reference osisRef="Amos.2.2">Amo 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.1">Jer 48:1</reference>, there is no mention of Ar. (2.) Kerioth is mentioned as an important place in the country in <reference osisRef="Amos.2.2">Amo 2:2</reference>, where, from the whole arrangement of the prophecy, it can only be the capital of Moab; in this present chapter also, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.24">Jer 48:24</reference>, Kerioth and Bozrah are introduced as two very important towns which maintained the strength of Moab; and immediately afterwards it is added, "The horn of Moab is cut off," etc. Further, in <reference osisRef="Jer.48.41">Jer 48:41</reference> the capture of Kerioth is put on a level with the taking of the fortresses; while it is added, that the courage of the mighty men has failed, just as in <reference osisRef="Jer.49.22">Jer 49:22</reference> the capture of Bozrah is coupled with the loss of courage on the part of Edom’s heroes. Bozrah is not to be confounded with Bozrah in Edom (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.13">Jer 49:13</reference>), nor with the later flourishing city of Bostra in Hauran: it is the same with Bezer (בּצר), which, according to <reference osisRef="Deut.4.43">Deu 4:43</reference> and <reference osisRef="Josh.20.8">Jos 20:8</reference>, was situated in the Mishor of the tribe of Reuben, but has not yet been discovered; see on Deu 4:43. For the purpose of completing the enumeration, it is further added, "all the towns of the land of Moab, those which are far off (i.e., those which are situated towards the frontier) and those which are near" (i.e., the towns of the interior, as Kimchi has already explained). Thereby the horn of Moab is cut off, and his arm broken. Horn and arm are figures of power: the horn an emblem of power that boldly asserts itself, and pushes down all that opposes (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.75.5">Psa 75:5</reference>, 11); the arm being rather an emblem of dominion.
entries.ee8e6789280c7f2893062a4ebe9b911101a1ca6a: <reference osisRef="Jer.48.26-Jer.48.27">Jer 48:26-27</reference> <hi type="italic">Moab’s haughtiness and deplorable fall. -</hi> Jer 48:26. <hi type="italic">"Make him drunk - for he hath boasted against Jahveh - so that Moab shall splash down into his vomit, and himself become a laughing-stock.</hi> Jer 48:27. <hi type="italic">Was not Israel a laughing-stock to thee, or was he found among thieves? for whenever thou spakest of him, thou didst shake thine head.</hi> Jer 48:28. <hi type="italic">Leave the cities and dwell in the rock, ye inhabitants of Moab; and be ye like a dove [that] builds its nest in the sides of the mouth of a pit.</hi> Jer 48:29. <hi type="italic">We have heard the very arrogant pride of Moab, his haughtiness, and his arrogance, and his high-mindedness, and his elation of mind.</hi> Jer 48:30. <hi type="italic">I know, saith Jahveh, his wrath, and the untruthfulness of his words; they have done what is untrue.</hi> Jer 48:31. <hi type="italic">Therefore will I howl over Moab, and for all Moab will I cry; they mourn for the people of Kir-heres.</hi> Jer 48:32. <hi type="italic">I will weep for thee [with more] than the weeping of Jazer, O vine of Sibmah, thou whose tendrils have gone over the sea, have reached even to the sea of Jazer; on thy fruit-harvest and thy vintage a spoiler has fallen.</hi> Jer 48:33. <hi type="italic">And joy and gladness are taken from the garden, and from the land of Moab; and I have caused wine to fail from the wine-vats: they shall not tread [with] a shout; the shout shall be no shout.</hi> Jer 48:34. <hi type="italic">From the cry of Heshbon as far as Elealeh, as far as Jahaz, they utter their voice; from Zoar as far as Horonaim and the third Eglath; for even the waters of Nimrim shall become desolations.</hi> Jer 48:35. <hi type="italic">And I will destroy from Moab, saith Jahveh, him that offers on a high place and burns incense to his gods."</hi> <div eID="gen14394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14395" type="x-p"/> Through his pride, Moab has incurred the sentence of destruction to his power. In arrogance and rage he has exalted himself over Jahveh and His people Israel; therefore must he now be humbled, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.26">Jer 48:26</reference>-30. The summons to make Moab drunk is addressed to those whom God has charged with the execution of the sentence; cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.48.10">Jer 48:10</reference> and Jer 48:21. These are to present to the people of Moab the cup of the divine wrath, and so to intoxicate them, that they shall fall like a drunk man into his vomit, and become a laughing-stock to others (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.13.13">Jer 13:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.15">Jer 25:15</reference>), because they have boasted against Jahveh by driving the Israelites from their inheritance, and by deriding the people of God; cf. Zep 2:8. ספק, to strike, frequently of striking the hands together; here it signifies to fall into his vomit, i.e., to tumble into it with a splash. No other explanation of the word can find support from the language used. Cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.19.14">Isa 19:14</reference> and Isa 25:10. In the last clause of <reference osisRef="Jer.48.26">Jer 48:26</reference>, the emphasis lies on גּם הוּא: "he also (Moab, like Israel before) shall become a laughing-stock." This statement is enforced by the question put in <reference osisRef="Jer.48.27">Jer 48:27</reference>, "Was not Israel a laughing-stock to thee?" ואם־אם shows a double question, like ה־אם; and ואם in the first clause may be further strengthened by the interrogative ה before שׂחק, as in Gen 17:17. For other forms of the double question, see <reference osisRef="Ps.94.9">Psa 94:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.21.4">Job 21:4</reference>; Jer 23:26. On <hi type="italic">Dagesh dirimens</hi> in השּׂחק, cf. Ewald, §104, <hi type="italic">b</hi>. There is no sufficient reason for questioning the feminine form נמצאה in the <hi type="italic">Qeri</hi>; Israel is personified as a woman, just as Moab in <reference osisRef="Jer.48.20">Jer 48:20</reference>, where חתּה is found. On מדּי דב, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.31.20">Jer 31:20</reference>, where, however, דּבּר בּ is used in another meaning. התנודד, to shake oneself, is a stronger expression than הניד בּראשׁ, to shake the head (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.16">Jer 18:16</reference>), a gesture denoting mockery and rejoicing over another’s injury; cf. Psa 64:9.
entries.a35e2faaa1825992a08e9953b883e54863c35865: <reference osisRef="Jer.48.28">Jer 48:28</reference> <div eID="gen14395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14396" type="x-p"/> A transition is now made from figurative to literal language, and Moab is summoned to leave the cities and take refuge in inaccessible rocks, because he will not be able to offer resistance to the enemy; cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.48.6">Jer 48:6</reference> and Jer 48:9. "Like a dove that builds its nest over deep crevices." The reference is to wild pigeons, which occur in large numbers in Palestine, and make their nests in the clefts of high rocks (Sol 2:14) even at the present day, e.g., in the wilderness of Engedi; cf. Robinson’s <hi type="italic">Palestine</hi>, ii. 203. בּעברי , lit., "on the other side of the mouth of the deep pit," or of the abyss, i.e., over the yawning hollows. בּעברי is a poetic form for בּעבר, as in Isa 7:20. The humiliation of Moab finds its justification in what is brought out in Jer 48:29., his boundless pride and hatred against Israel.
entries.7ad86026d9258543d60a6a530339f19476ecc567: <reference osisRef="Jer.48.29-Jer.48.30">Jer 48:29-30</reference> <div eID="gen14396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14397" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Jer.48.29">Jer 48:29</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.48.30">Jer 48:30</reference> only more fully develop the idea contained in Isa 16:6. Those who "heard" are the prophet and the people of God. There is an accumulation of words to describe the pride of Moab. Isaiah’s expression also, עברתו לא־כן בּדּיו, is here expanded into two clauses, and Jahveh is named as the subject. Not only have the people of God perceived the pride of Moab, but God also knows his wrath. בּדּיו belongs to לא־כן as a genitive, as in Isaiah לא־כן means "not right," contrary to actual facts, i.e., untrue.<note placement="foot">The Masoretic accentuation, according to which Athnach is placed under כּן, exhibits another view of the words in the text: this is shown by the Chaldee paraphrase, "their nobles endure not, they have not done what is right." The Masoretes took בּדּים in the sense of "staves," and took staves as a symbol of princes, as in Hos 11:6. Luther, in his translation, "I know his anger well, that he cannot do so very much, and attempts to do more than he can," follows the Vulgate, <hi type="italic">Ego scio jactantiam ejus, et quod non sit juxta eam virtus ejus, nec juxta quod poterat conata sit facere</hi>, which again seems to have followed the lxx in taking בּדיּו for בּדּיו.</note> <div eID="gen14397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14398" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Jer.48.31-Jer.48.33">Jer 48:31-33</reference> are also an imitation of <reference osisRef="Isa.16.7">Isa 16:7</reference>-10. V. 31 is a reproduction of Isa 16:7. In <reference osisRef="Jer.48.7">Jer 48:7</reference>, Isaiah sets forth the lamentation of Moab over the devastation of his country and its precious fruits; and not until v. 9 does the prophet, in deep sympathy, mingle his tears with those of the Moabites. Jeremiah, on the other hand, with his natural softness, at once begins, in the first person, his lament over Moab. על־כּן, "therefore," is not immediately connected with Jer 48:29., but with the leading idea presented in <reference osisRef="Jer.48.26">Jer 48:26</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.48.28">Jer 48:28</reference>, that Moab will fall like one intoxicated, and that he must flee out of his cities. If we refer it to <reference osisRef="Jer.48.30">Jer 48:30</reference>, there we must attach it to the thought implicitly contained in the emphatic statement, "I (Jahveh) know his wrath," viz., "and I will punish him for it." The <hi type="italic">I</hi> who makes lament is the prophet, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.16.9">Isa 16:9</reference> and Isa 15:5. Schnurrer, Hitzig, and Graf, on the contrary, think that it is an indefinite third person who is introduced as representing the Moabites; but there is no analogous case to support this assumption, since the instances in which third persons are introduced are of a different kind. But when Graf further asserts, against referring the <hi type="italic">I</hi> to the prophet, that, according to what precedes, especially what we find in Jer 48:26., such an outburst of sympathy for Moab would involve a contradiction, he makes out the prophet to be a Jew thirsting for revenge, which he was not. Raschi has already well remarked, on the other hand, under <reference osisRef="Isa.15.5">Isa 15:5</reference>, that "the prophets of Israel differ from heathen prophets like Balaam in this, that they lay to heart the distress which they announce to the nations;" cf. Isa 21:3. The prophet weeps for all Moab, because the judgment is coming not merely on the northern portion (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.18-Jer.48.25">Jer 48:18-25</reference>), but on the whole of the country. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Jer.48.31">Jer 48:31</reference></hi>, Jeremiah has properly changed לאשׁישׁי (cakes of dried grapes) into אל־אנשׁי, the people of Kir-heres, because his sympathy was directed, not to dainties, but to the men in Moab; he has also omitted "surely they are smitten," as being too strong for his sympathy. יהגּה, to groan, taken from the cooing of doves, perhaps after <reference osisRef="Isa.38.15">Isa 38:15</reference>; Isa 59:11. The third person indicates a universal indefinite. Kir-heres, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.16.11">Isa 16:11</reference>, or Kir-haresheth in <reference osisRef="Isa.16.7">Isa 16:7</reference>; 2Ki 3:25, was the chief stronghold of Moab, probably the same as Kir-Moab, the modern Kerek, as we may certainly infer from a comparison of <reference osisRef="Isa.16.7">Isa 16:7</reference> with <reference osisRef="Isa.15.1">Isa 15:1</reference> see on 2Ki 3:25, and Dietrich, S. 324.
entries.8426a406ed83c8f07466e3aa0113962076463383: <reference osisRef="Jer.48.32-Jer.48.33">Jer 48:32-33</reference> מבּכי יעזר, "more than the weeping of Jazer," may signify, "More than Jazer weeps do I weep over thee;" or, "More than over Jazer weeps do I weep over thee;" or, "More than over Jazer do I weep over thee." However, the former interpretation is the more obvious, and is confirmed by the reading in Isa 16:9. According to the <hi type="italic">Onomasticon</hi>, Jazer was fifteen Roman miles north from Heshbon. Seetzen recognises it in the ruins called es Szir at the source of the <hi type="italic">Nahr Szir</hi>; see on Num 21:32. According to Jerome, on <reference osisRef="Isa.16.8">Isa 16:8</reference>, Sibmah was only five hundred paces from Heshbon; see on Num 32:38. Judging from the verse now before us, and from Isa. <hi type="italic">l.c.</hi>, the vines of Sibmah must have been famed for the strength and excellence of their clusters. Even now, that region produces excellent grapes in abundance. From Szalt, which lies only ten miles north from Szir, raisins and grapes are carried to Jerusalem, and these of excellent quality (Seetzen, i. S. 399; Burckhardt, p. 350). In what follows, "his tendrils crossed the sea," etc., the extensive cultivation of the grape is set forth under the figure of a vine whose tendrils stretch out on all sides. "They have crossed over the sea" has reference in Isaiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.8">Isa 16:8</reference>) to the Dead Sea (ים, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.23">Psa 68:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.2">2Ch 20:2</reference>); not merely, however, in the sense of the shoots reaching close to the Dead Sea, but also over it, for Engedi was famed for its vines (Sol 1:14). Jeremiah also has reproduced the words taken from Isaiah in this sense. From the following clause, "they reached to the sea of Jazer," it does not follow that he has specified "the sea" by "Jazer." What tells rather the other way is the fact that עבר, which means to cross over, cannot possibly be used as equivalent to נגע עד, "to reach to." "They crossed over the sea" shows extension towards the west, while "they reached to the sea of Jazer" indicates extension towards the north. This latter statement also is an imitation of what we find in <reference osisRef="Isa.16.8">Isa 16:8</reference>; and "Jazer" is merely further specified as "the sea of Jazer." In spite of the most diligent inquiries, Seetzen (i. S. 406) could learn nothing from the people of that region regarding an inland lake; but in the beautiful green vale in the vicinity of Szâr (i.e., Jazer) there were several ponds, which he supposes may possibly be the <hi type="italic">mare Jazer</hi>, since this valley lying among the mountains is somewhat depressed, and in ancient times was probably filled with water. The "sea" (ים) of Solomon’s temple further shows that ים does not necessarily denote only a large lake, but might also be applied to a large artificial basin of water. So also, at the present day, the artificial water-basins on the streets of Damascus are called <hi type="italic">baharat</hi>, "seas;" cf. Wetzstein in Delitzsch on Isa 16:8. This cultivation of the vine is at an end; for the destroyer has fallen upon the fruit-harvest and the vintage. Jeremiah, by "the destroyer has fallen," explains the words of Isaiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.9">Isa 16:9</reference>), "shouting has fallen." - In <reference osisRef="Jer.48.33">Jer 48:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.16.10">Isa 16:10</reference> is reproduced. "Joy and gladness are taken away from the gardens, and from the whole land of Moab." כּרמל is not here a proper name, for Mount Carmel does not at all suit the present context; it is an appellative, fruit-land, i.e., the fruitful wine-country near Jazer. Jeremiah adds, "and from the land (i.e., the whole land) of Moab." The pressing of the grapes comes to an end; there is no wine in the vat; no longer is the wine pressed with "Hedad." הידד is an adverbial accusative. This is further specified by the oxymoron: a "<hi type="italic">Hedad</hi>, and yet not a <hi type="italic">Hedad</hi>." This word generally signifies any loud shout, - not merely the shout of the wine-pressers as they tread the grapes (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.25.30">Jer 25:30</reference>), but also a battle-cry; cf. Jer 51:14. Hence the meaning is, "<hi type="italic">Hedad</hi> is heard, but not a merry shout of the wine-pressers." <div eID="gen14398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14399" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Jer.48.34">Jer 48:34</reference> is based on <reference osisRef="Isa.15.4">Isa 15:4</reference>-6. "From the cry of Heshbon is heard the echo as far as Elealeh and Jahaz," or "from Heshbon to Elealeh and Jahaz is heard a cry, and from Zoar to Horonaim." Heshbon and Elealeh are only about two miles distant from each other; their ruins are still visible under the names of <hi type="italic">Hesbân</hi> (Husban, see on <reference osisRef="Jer.48.2">Jer 48:2</reference>) and <hi type="italic">El Al</hi> (see on Num 32:37). They were both built on hills; Elealeh in particular was situated on the summit of a hill whence the whole of the southern Belka may be seen (Burckhardt, p. 365), so that a shout thence emitted could be heard at a great distance, even as far as Jahaz, which is pretty far off to the south-west from Heshbon (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.48.21">Jer 48:21</reference>). The words "from Zoar to Horonaim" also depend on "they uttered their voice." Both places lay in the south of the land; see on <reference osisRef="Jer.48.3">Jer 48:3</reference> and Jer 48:4. The wailing resounds not merely on the north, but also on the south of the Arnon. There is much dispute as to the meaning of עגלת  שׁלישׁיּה, which is here mentioned after Horonaim, but in <reference osisRef="Isa.15.5">Isa 15:5</reference> in connection with, or after Zoar. To take the expression as an appellative, <hi type="italic">juvenca tertii anni</hi> (lxx, Vulgate, Targum, Gesenius, etc.), would perhaps be suitable, if it were an apposition to Moab, in which case we might compare with it passages like <reference osisRef="Jer.46.20">Jer 46:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.11">Jer 50:11</reference>; but this does not accord with its position after Horonaim and Zoar, for we have no analogy for the comparison of cities or fortresses with <hi type="italic">a juvenca tertii anni, h. e. indomita jugoque non assueta</hi>; and it cannot even be proved that Zoar and Horonaim were fortresses of Moab. Hence we take 'עגלת שׁ as the proper name of a place, "the third Eglath;" this is the view of Rosenmüller, Drechsler, and Dietrich (in <hi type="italic">Merx' Archiv.</hi> i. S. 342ff.). The main reason for this view, is, that there would be no use for an addition being made, by way of apposition, to a place which is mentioned as the limit of the Moabites’ flight, or that reached by their wailing. The parallelism of the clauses argues in favour of its being a proper name; for, on this view of it, three towns are named in both members, the first one, as the starting-point of the cry of wailing, the other two as points up to which it is heard. The preposition עד, which is omitted, may be supplied from the parallel member, as in Isa 15:8. Regarding the position of <hi type="italic">Eglath Shelishijah</hi>, it is evident from the context of both passages that we must look for it on the southern frontier of Moab. It is implied in the epithet "the third" that there were three places (villages), not far from one another, all bearing the same name. Dietrich (S. 344f.) has adduced several analogous cases of towns in the country to the east of the Jordan, - two, and sometimes even three, towns of the same name, which are distinguished from each other by numerals. "The waters of Nimrim also shall become desolations," because the enemy fill up the springs with earth. Nimrim is not the place called נמרה or בּית נמרה mentioned in Num 32:3, Num 32:36; <reference osisRef="Josh.13.27">Jos 13:27</reference>, whose ruins lie on the way from Szalt to Jericho, in the Wady Shaib, on the east side of the Jordan (see on Num 32:36), for this lies much too far to the north to be the place mentioned here. The context points to a place in the south, in Moab proper. where Burckhardt (p. 355), Seetzen (<hi type="italic">Reisen</hi>, ii. S. 354), and de Saulcy (<hi type="italic">Voyage</hi>, i. 283, ii. 52) have indicated a stream fed by a spring, called <hi type="italic">Moiet Numêre</hi> (i.e., brook Nimrah), in the country at the south end of the Dead Sea, and in that wady a mass of ruins called <hi type="italic">Numêre</hi> (the <hi type="italic">Nimmery</hi> of Seetzen, iii. 18).
entries.6d7c1965dec7b60958caad381400ad7230b1c9d9: <reference osisRef="Jer.48.35">Jer 48:35</reference> <div eID="gen14399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14400" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Jer.48.35">Jer 48:35</reference> ends the strophe of which it is a part; here the Lord declares that He will make to cease למואב (for, or from Moab, lit., to Moab), every one who offers on a high place and burns incense to his gods. מעלה cannot be a substantive, else the parallelism would be destroyed. Nor may we, with Hitzig, render "he who raises a high place," i.e., builds it, for העלה is not used in this sense.
entries.4b52b37f97f8350eb7ebd90dc400ed8c54c089da: <reference osisRef="Jer.48.36">Jer 48:36</reference> <hi type="italic">Further lamentation over the fall of Moab.</hi> - Jer 48:36. <hi type="italic">"Therefore my heart sounds like pipes for Moab, and my heart sounds like pipes for the men of Kir-heres; therefore the savings which he has made are perished. </hi> Jer 48:37. <hi type="italic">For every head is baldness, and every beard is shorn; on all hands there are cuts, and on loins sackcloth. </hi> Jer 48:38. <hi type="italic">On all the roofs of Moab, and in its streets, it is all mourning; for I have broken Moab like a vessel, in which there is no pleasure, saith Jahveh."</hi> <div eID="gen14400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14401" type="x-p"/> The prophet once more lifts up his lamentation over Moab (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.36">Jer 48:36</reference> corresponds to <reference osisRef="Jer.48.31">Jer 48:31</reference>), and gives reason for it in the picture he draws of the deep affliction of the Moabites. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Jer.48.36">Jer 48:36</reference></hi> is an imitation of <reference osisRef="Isa.16.11">Isa 16:11</reference>; the thought presented in v. 36 <hi type="italic">b</hi> accords with that found in Isa 15:7. Isaiah says, "My bowels sound (groan) like the harp," whose strings give a tremulous sound when struck with the plectrum. Instead of this, Jeremiah puts the sounding of pipes, the instruments used in dirges (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.23">Mat 9:23</reference>). Moab and Kir-heres are mentioned together, as in Jer 48:31. על־כּן, in the second clause, does not stand for כּי על־כּן, "on this account that" (Kimchi, Hitzig, Graf, etc.), but is co-ordinated with the first על־כּן. The idea is not, "Therefore my heart mourns over Moab, because the savings are perished;" but because the sentence of desolation has been passed on the whole of Moab, therefore the heart of the prophet makes lament, and therefore, too, all the property which Moab has acquired is lost. יתרה, as a collective noun, is joined with the plural verb אבדוּ. On the construction יתרת עשׂה, cf. Gesenius, §123, 3, Rem. 1; Ewald, §332, <hi type="italic">c</hi>. The proof of this is given by the deep sorrow and wailing of the whole Moabite nation, Jer 48:37. On all sides are tokens of the deepest sadness, - heads shorn bald, beards cut off, incisions on the hands, sackcloth round the loins.
entries.f305e4a1bd024233a795d5deee644bdc1154fc28: <reference osisRef="Jer.48.37-Jer.48.38">Jer 48:37-38</reference> <div eID="gen14401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14402" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Jer.48.37">Jer 48:37</reference> is formed out of pieces taken from <reference osisRef="Isa.15.2">Isa 15:2</reference>-3. קרחה is a substantive, "baldness," i.e., quite bald. גּרוּעה, <hi type="italic">decurtata</hi>, instead of גּדוּעה (in Isaiah), is weaker, but more suitable for the present connection. גּדדת, i.e., cuts or scratches inflicted on the body, as signs of mourning; cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.16.6">Jer 16:6</reference>; Jer 41:5. כּלּה , "It is all wailing;" nothing is heard but wailing, for God has broken Moab in pieces like a useless vessel. On the simile employed, cf. Jer 22:28.
entries.c44c0fa18cb38141a5782b8ed30808cf2ac5e3ec: <reference osisRef="Jer.48.39-Jer.48.44">Jer 48:39-44</reference> <hi type="italic">No escape from destruction.</hi> - Jer 48:39. <hi type="italic">"How it is broken! they howl. How hath Moab turned the back, for shame! And Moab becomes a laughing-stock and a terror to all his neighbours. </hi> Jer 48:40. <hi type="italic">For thus saith Jahveh: Behold, he shall fly like the eagle, and spread his wings over Moab. </hi> Jer 48:41. <hi type="italic">Kerioth is taken, and the strongholds are seized, and the heart of the heroes of Moab on that day become like the heart of a travailing woman. </hi> Jer 48:42. <hi type="italic">And Moab is destroyed from being a people, because he hath boasted against Jahveh. </hi> Jer 48:43. <hi type="italic">Fear, and a pit, and a snare, are against thee, O inhabitants of Moab, saith Jahveh. </hi> Jer 48:44. <hi type="italic">He who flees from the fear shall fall into the pit, and he who goes up out of the pit shall be taken in the snare; for I will bring against it, against Moab, the year of their recompense, saith Jahveh."</hi> <div eID="gen14402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14403" type="x-p"/> The subject of חתּה in <reference osisRef="Jer.48.39">Jer 48:39</reference> is Moab viewed as a nation. הילילוּ might be imperative, but in this case we would be obliged to take בּושׁ also as an imperative (as Hitzig and Graf do). It is simpler to take both forms as perfects: "they howl...Moab turns the back, is ashamed" (= for shame). On היה לשׂחק, cf. Jer 48:26. מחתּה, object of terror, as in Jer 17:17. "All who are round about him," as in Jer 48:17. "For (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.40">Jer 48:40</reference>) the enemy rushes down upon Moab like an eagle, and seizes Kerioth and all his strongholds." The subject is left unnamed, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.46.18">Jer 46:18</reference>, but it is Nebuchadnezzar. The figure of the eagle, darting down in flight on its prey, is founded on <reference osisRef="Deut.28.49">Deu 28:49</reference> (on אל- for על, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.49.22">Jer 49:22</reference>). Kerioth, the capital, is taken (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.48.24">Jer 48:24</reference>); so are the other strongholds or fastnesses of the country. The mere fact that קריּות has the article does not justify any one in taking it as an appellative, "the cities;" this appears from a comparison of <reference osisRef="Amos.2.2">Amo 2:2</reference> with this verse. No plural of קריה occurs anywhere. Then the fear of death falls on the heroes of Moab like a woman in labour. מצרה, partic. Hiphil from צרר, <hi type="italic">uterum comprimens</hi>, is found only here and in <reference osisRef="Jer.49.22">Jer 49:22</reference>, where the figure is repeated. Moab is annihilated, so that it is no longer a nation (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.48.2">Jer 48:2</reference>), because it has risen up in pride against the God of Israel; cf. Jer 48:26. He who flees from one danger falls into the other. The play on the words פּחד, fear, horror, פּחת, pit, and פּח, spring-trap, as well as the mode in which it is carried out, is taken from Isa 24:17., - a prophecy of the judgment on the world; see a similar idea presented in <reference osisRef="Amos.5.19">Amo 5:19</reference>, but somewhat differently expressed. The <hi type="italic">Kethib</hi> הניס, perfect Hiphil, "he flees," is less suitable than the <hi type="italic">Qeri</hi> הנּס (after Isaiah). The last clause, "for I will bring," etc., is quite in Jeremiah’s peculiar style; cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.4.23">Jer 4:23</reference>; Jer 23:12. אליה belongs to אל־מואב: the noun is anticipated by the pronoun, as frequently occurs; cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.9.14">Jer 9:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.41.3">Jer 41:3</reference>; Jer 43:11.
entries.f6e1173c8a2bba175a778c138936befeba9e68d3: <reference osisRef="Jer.48.45-Jer.48.47">Jer 48:45-47</reference> <hi type="italic">Conclusion</hi>. - Jer 48:45. <hi type="italic">"Under the shadow of Heshbon stand fugitives, powerless; for a fire goes out from Heshbon, and a flame from Sihon, and devours the region of Moab, and the crown of the head of the sons of tumult. </hi> Jer 48:46. <hi type="italic">Woe unto thee, Moab! the people of Chemosh are perished! for thy sons are taken away into captivity, and thy daughters into captivity. </hi> Jer 48:47. <hi type="italic">Yet will I turn the captivity of Moab at the end of the days, saith Jahveh. Thus far is the judgment of Moab."</hi> <div eID="gen14403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14404" type="x-p"/> From Heshbon issued the resolution to annihilate Moab (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.2">Jer 48:2</reference>); to Heshbon the prophecy finally returns. "In the shadow of Heshbon stand fugitives, powerless’ (מכּח, with מן privative), where, no doubt, they were seeking refuge; cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.30.2">Isa 30:2</reference>-3. The fugitives can only be Moabites. Here it is astonishing that they seek refuge in Heshbon, since the enemy comes from the north, and according to <reference osisRef="Jer.48.2">Jer 48:2</reference>, it is in Heshbon that the resolution to destroy Moab was formed; and judging from <reference osisRef="Jer.49.3">Jer 49:3</reference>, that city was then in the hands of the Ammonites. Hence Hitzig and Graf miss the connection. Hitzig thinks that the whole clause was inserted by a glosser, who imagined the town belonged to Moab, perhaps allowing himself to be misled in this by Num 21:27, "Come to Heshbon." Graf, on the other hand, is of opinion that the fugitives are seeking the protection of the Ammonites in Heshbon, but do not find it: hence he would take the כּי which follows in the adversative sense of "however" or "rather;" but this is against the use of the word, and cannot be allowed. The tenor of the words, "Fugitives stand under the shadow of Heshbon," does not require us to assume that people had fled to Heshbon out of the whole of Moab. Let us rather think of fugitives from the environs of Heshbon, who seek refuge in this fortified town, from the enemy advancing from the north, but who find themselves disappointed in their expectation, because from this city there bursts forth the fire of war which destroys Moab. The thought merely serves the purpose of attaching to it the utterances which follow regarding Moab; but from <reference osisRef="Jer.48.43">Jer 48:43</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.48.44">Jer 48:44</reference> alone, it is evident that escape will be impossible. In proof of this he mentions the flight to Heshbon, that he may have an opportunity of introducing a portion of the old triumphal songs of the Mosaic age, with which he wished to conclude his prophecy, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Jer.48.45">Jer 48:45</reference></hi> and Jer 48:46. The fugitives stand powerless, i.e., exhausted and unable to flee any further, while Heshbon affords them no refuge. For there bursts forth from it the fire that is to destroy the whole of Moab. The words from "for a fire," etc., on to the end of <reference osisRef="Jer.48.46">Jer 48:46</reference>, are a free imitation of some strophes out of an ancient song, in which poets of the Mosaic period celebrated the victory of Israel over Sihon the king of the Amorites, who had conquered the greater portion of Moab; but with this here is interwoven a passage from the utterances of Balaam the seer, regarding the fall of Moab, found in Num 24:17, viz., from ותּאכל to בּני שׁאון. These insertions are made for the purpose of showing that, through this judgment which is now coming upon Moab, not only those ancient sayings, but also the prophecy of Balaam, will find their full accomplishment. Just as in the time of Moses, so now also there again proceeds from Heshbon the fire of war which will consume Moab. The words, "for a fire has gone out from Heshbon," are a verbatim repetition of what we find in Num 21:28, with the single exception that אשׁ is here, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.104.4">Psa 104:4</reference>, construed as masculine, and thus takes יצא instead of יצאה; but this change, of course, does not affect the meaning of the words. The next clause runs, in Numbers, <hi type="italic">l.c.</hi>, להבה מקּרית סיחון, but here ולהבה מבּין; this change into מבּין is difficult to account for, so that J. D. Michaelis and Ewald would alter it into מבּית. <div eID="gen14404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14405" type="x-p"/> There is no need for refuting the assumption of Raschi and Nägelsbach, that Sihon stands for the city of Sihon; or the fancy of Morus and Hitzig, that an old glosser imagined Sihon was a town instead of a king. When we consider that the burning of Heshbon by the Israelites, celebrated in that ancient song, was brought on by Sihon the Amorite king, since the Israelites were not to make war on Moab, and only fought against Sihon, who had made Heshbon his residence, there can be no doubt that Jeremiah purposely changed מקּרית into מבּין סיחון, in order to show that Sihon was the originator of the fire which consumed Heshbon. By this latter expression Jeremiah seeks to intimate that, in Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldean army, there will arise against the Moabites another Sihon, from whose legions will burst forth the flame that is to consume Moab. מבּין, "from between," is to be explained on the ground that Sion is not viewed as a single individual, but as the leader of martial hosts. This fire will "devour the region of Moab, and the crown of the head of the sons of tumult." These words have been taken by Jeremiah from Balaam’s utterance regarding Moab, Num 24:17, and embodied in his address after some transformation.
